how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '(443|8443|4433|8883)'; nft list ruleset | grep -E '(443|8443|4433|8883)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules explicitly allowing only management server IP ranges to communicate on the update port, with a default-deny policy for all other sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On network devices (Cisco IOS/IOS-XE), display the access control lists applied to interfaces carrying management update traffic and verify permit entries are scoped to authorized management server and endpoint subnets only.
how_to_obtain.command: show ip access-lists | include -A (permit|deny); show running-config | section ip access-list
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Named or numbered ACLs with explicit permit statements for management server CIDRs and endpoint management subnets, terminated by an implicit or explicit deny any any.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud environments (AWS/Azure/GCP), navigate to the security group or network security group associated with management server instances. Review inbound and outbound rules on the management update port to confirm only authorized CIDR ranges or security group IDs are permitted.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → EC2 → Security Groups → [Management Server SG] → Inbound Rules; Azure Portal → Network Security Groups → [Management NSG] → Inbound Security Rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules scoped to specific management CIDR ranges or security group references on the update port, with no 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 permit rules on that port.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the AWS EC2 API or Azure REST API to programmatically enumerate security group rules for management server resources and verify ACL scope.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing IpRanges or UserIdGroupPairs entries scoped to authorized management subnets on the relevant management port, without wildcard 0.0.0.0/0 entries.

option_description: Indicates whether configuration update payloads transmitted over the management channel are compressed using algorithms such as DEFLATE, gzip, or zstd, either at the TLS layer (via TLS compression extensions) or at the application layer (HTTP Content-Encoding headers or middleware compression). Compression applied before or during encryption exposes the channel to length-based oracle attacks.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'update_payload_compression_oracle_attack' exposure only when payload_compression_enabled is true AND attacker_can_inject_partial_content is true AND ciphertext_length_observable is true. This models CRIME (TLS-layer compression) and BREACH (HTTP-layer compression) attack classes. When all three conditions are met, an attacker can iteratively submit requests with injected known plaintext and observe whether compressed-then-encrypted response lengths decrease, enabling byte-by-byte recovery of sensitive configuration values such as tokens or credentials within the payload. Setting this to false eliminates the compression oracle precondition entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use OpenSSL to perform a TLS handshake with the management server and inspect whether TLS-layer compression is negotiated (indicated by 'Compression: zlib compression' in the handshake output).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If compression is disabled, output should show 'Compression: NONE'. Any other value (e.g., 'zlib compression') indicates TLS-layer compression is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use curl to send a configuration update request to the management endpoint and examine response headers for Content-Encoding to detect application-layer compression (gzip, deflate, br, zstd).
how_to_obtain.command: curl -v -k --cert client.pem --key client.key -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br' https://<mgmt-server>:<port>/api/config/update 2>&1 | grep -i 'content-encoding'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of Content-Encoding header indicates no application-layer compression. Presence of 'Content-Encoding: gzip' or similar confirms compression is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the management server application configuration for compression middleware or OpenSSL compilation options that enable compression. Check web server config files (nginx, Apache) for gzip/brotli directives on the management endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No active gzip_on, BrotliOn, or equivalent compression directives on the management update endpoint location blocks. Directives should be explicitly set to 'off' or absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the management server's OpenSSL build includes compression support, which would allow TLS compression to be negotiated if not explicitly disabled in application code.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl version -a | grep -i 'zlib\|compress'; python3 -c "import ssl; ctx=ssl.create_default_context(); print(ctx.options)" 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OpenSSL built without zlib indicates TLS compression is unavailable. If zlib is present, application-level configuration must explicitly disable TLS compression via SSL_OP_NO_COMPRESSION.

option_description: Determines whether an attacker can influence or inject partial known plaintext into the compressed-then-encrypted configuration update payload. This capability can arise through cross-origin request forgery (CORS misconfigurations allowing attacker-controlled pages to trigger update requests), server-side request forgery (SSRF) into the management channel, partial update API fields that accept attacker-supplied values merged into the payload, or other injection vectors that allow the attacker to control portions of what gets compressed alongside secrets.
security_impact: The Rego policy requires attacker_can_inject_partial_content to be true (alongside payload_compression_enabled and ciphertext_length_observable) to fire the 'update_payload_compression_oracle_attack' exposure. This attribute represents the active attacker capability that makes compression oracle attacks practical: without the ability to inject known plaintext strings into the compressed payload, the attacker cannot use the length oracle to recover secret values. Injection vectors include CORS-bypassed cross-origin fetch calls to the update endpoint, SSRF that proxies attacker content through the management server, or partial update API calls that merge attacker-controlled field values alongside secret tokens in the same compressed payload.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test CORS policy on the management update endpoint by sending a cross-origin preflight and simple request with an attacker-controlled Origin header. If the server reflects the origin or returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, attacker-controlled pages can trigger authenticated update requests.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure deployments return no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header or restrict it to the exact management console origin. A wildcard (*) or reflected attacker origin indicates CORS-based injection is possible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the management server API specification and source code or documentation for any partial update endpoints (PATCH /config, PUT /config/field) that accept attacker-influenced values and merge them with sensitive fields (tokens, credentials, policy secrets) before compression and encryption.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review API documentation at https://<mgmt-server>/api/docs or inspect source code in the config update handler for field merging logic prior to compression.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Partial update endpoints should not merge attacker-controlled field values with secret fields in the same compression context. If they do, this confirms the injection vector exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Probe for SSRF vulnerabilities in the management server by submitting configuration update requests with URL or host fields that reference internal endpoints, testing whether the server fetches attacker-controlled content and merges it into a subsequent compressed update payload.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the server does not fetch the external URL and returns an error rejecting external config sources, SSRF injection is not present. HTTP requests hitting the attacker-controlled server confirm SSRF.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect management server CORS configuration and middleware chain to identify whether any middleware merges request body parameters with sensitive configuration context before passing to the compression layer.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CORS configuration should list explicit allowed origins matching only the management console domain. No middleware should merge request-supplied values with secrets in the same compression buffer.

option_description: Determines whether an attacker in a position to observe network traffic (on-path or on a shared segment) can measure the byte length of encrypted configuration update responses. Length observability is the core requirement for CRIME/BREACH-class compression oracle attacks because the oracle signal is the change in ciphertext length as the compression ratio changes with injected known plaintext. Length may be observable via packet capture on a shared network segment, HTTP Content-Length response headers visible before TLS termination artifacts, Transfer-Encoding: chunked chunk sizes, or side-channel timing/length information in API responses.
security_impact: The Rego policy requires ciphertext_length_observable to be true (alongside payload_compression_enabled and attacker_can_inject_partial_content) to trigger the 'update_payload_compression_oracle_attack' exposure. If an attacker cannot observe ciphertext lengths, the compression oracle attack cannot proceed regardless of whether compression is enabled. Mitigations include fixed-length padding of all encrypted responses (making all responses the same length regardless of plaintext content), traffic shaping to prevent length inference, or ensuring attackers cannot be on-path to observe TLS record sizes. Assessors should determine both whether an attacker can achieve on-path positioning on the management network segment and whether the protocol exposes length information in observable metadata.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a network position on the same segment as the management channel (or via a port mirror), capture configuration update response traffic with tcpdump and measure TLS record lengths across multiple requests with varying payload content to determine if length variation is observable.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i <interface> -nn -s 0 'host <mgmt-server> and tcp port <mgmt-port>' -w /tmp/mgmt_capture.pcap; tshark -r /tmp/mgmt_capture.pcap -T fields -e tcp.len -e ssl.record.length | sort -u
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fixed-length or padded responses will show uniform TLS record lengths regardless of payload variation. Varying record lengths proportional to payload content confirm length observability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management update endpoint directly and inspect HTTP response headers for Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding: chunked with observable chunk sizes that reveal payload length even within a TLS session.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure deployments either use fixed-length padding (all responses same Content-Length) or omit Content-Length with chunked encoding designed to obscure payload size. Variable Content-Length values across requests with different payloads confirm length observability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network topology and segmentation controls for the management update channel to determine whether unauthorized or partially trusted hosts share the same network segment and could capture traffic via ARP spoofing, rogue switch port mirroring, or shared wireless media.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review network architecture diagrams, VLAN assignments, and switch port security configurations for the management server's network segment. Interview network operations staff about who has physical or logical access to the segment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Management server should reside on a dedicated isolated VLAN/segment accessible only to authorized management infrastructure, making on-path packet capture infeasible for untrusted parties.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the management server or its TLS terminator applies fixed-length padding or uses a transport that hides payload length (e.g., QUIC with padding frames, or application-level response padding configuration).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration explicitly setting fixed response padding or constant-length responses indicates length observability is mitigated. Absence of any padding configuration combined with variable Content-Length confirms the observable condition.
